title: Read/Write Through
subtitle: Inline caching abstractions where the cache layer sits directly in the data access path and coordinates database persistence.
keyTakeaways: In Read-Through and Write-Through caching, the application interacts solely with the cache abstraction, treating it as the primary data store.
Write-Through caching writes synchronously to both the cache and the database before acknowledging success, guaranteeing consistency at the cost of higher write latency.
While simplifying application code, Write-Through caches can pollute memory with rarely-read data unless paired with aggressive LRU eviction or write-around policies.
architectureDiagram:
INLINE CACHING ARCHITECTURE (Read-Through & Write-Through)
READ PATH:
  [ App Server ] --- 1. GET key ---> [ Cache Layer ]
                                           |
                                           +--- 2. On Miss: SELECT ---> [ Database ]
                                           +--- 3. Populates Cache & Returns Data

WRITE PATH (Synchronous Write-Through):
  [ App Server ] --- 1. PUT key ---> [ Cache Layer ]
                                           |
                                           +--- 2. Synchronous UPDATE -> [ Database ]
                                           +--- 3. Updates Cache Memory
                                           +--- 4. Returns 200 OK to App Server

sections.heading: How Read-Through and Write-Through Operate Together
sections.body: Unlike Cache-Aside where the application explicitly manages two separate network clients (Redis and the DB), inline caching abstracts the database behind the cache interface. The application treats the cache as the authoritative system of record. On reads, the cache handles cache misses transparently by querying the database. On writes, the cache writes data synchronously to both in-memory storage and the backing database before returning success.
bullets: Simplified Application Logic: Business services contain zero database fetch or fallback boilerplate; code interacts with a single unified data client.
Synchronous Consistency: Eliminates the stale read race condition found in naive cache-aside implementations because the cache layer serializes writes to both tiers.
Write Latency Overhead: Write latency is the sum of memory update latency and database disk fsync latency.

sections.heading: Handling Partial Failures and Cache Pollution
sections.body: The primary challenge in Write-Through caching is managing partial failures. If the cache update succeeds but the database write fails due to a constraint violation, the cache holds phantom data. Conversely, if the database write succeeds but the cache write fails, the cache serves stale data until eviction.
bullets: Database First: Always commit to durable persistent storage first; if the database transaction fails, abort immediately before updating cache memory.
Cache Pollution Risk: Writing every single mutation into cache memory means high-volume batch imports or write-heavy tables can flush active hot data out of RAM.

Write-Around Alternative: For datasets with low read-to-write ratios (such as audit logs or telemetry), bypass the cache on writes entirely ('Write-Around') and let data populate lazily on first read.

tradeOffs.pros: Cache is always fresh immediately following writes; completely abstracts database interactions from application microservices.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher write latency (must wait for synchronous DB commit); high memory churn if written data is rarely read.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Read-heavy entities with frequent read-after-write access patterns (user profile preferences, auth permissions).

tradeOffs.pros: Prevents cache memory pollution from bulk writes; preserves RAM for frequently accessed hot datasets.
tradeOffs.cons: First read after a write always encounters a cache miss and pays full database query latency.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time logging, analytical events, invoice archives, and historical record generation.

interviewTip: Distinguish between Write-Through and Write-Behind: 'Write-Through writes synchronously to both the cache and database before returning, ensuring zero data loss. Write-Behind acknowledges the write immediately to RAM and flushes to the database asynchronously, maximizing throughput at the risk of losing recent writes if the cache crashes.'
